subject: botany_2
question_text: Write the important features of the genetic code.

mark_split.label: Universal, with a start and stops

insider_note: Every feature has a NAME — triplet, unambiguous, degenerate, non-overlapping, comma-less, universal. Use the names; a description without the name reads as a guess.

steps.label: Triplet and the codon count
steps.margin_note: The triplet nature, the arithmetic, and the 61-and-3 split.
lines: 1. The genetic code is a TRIPLET code: three
bases on the mRNA specify one amino acid.
Each triplet is called a CODON.
2. There are 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 codons in all.
61 codons code for the 20 amino acids.
3 codons code for none — they are STOP codons.
steps.why: Four bases taken two at a time give only sixteen combinations, too few for twenty amino acids, so the code must be at least a triplet.
common_mistakes: Saying there are 64 amino acids. There are 64 CODONS and 20 amino acids.
Saying all 64 code for amino acids. THREE are stop codons.
steps.memory_tip: Four bases, three at a time: sixty-four codons for twenty amino acids.

steps.label: Unambiguous and degenerate
steps.margin_note: Both terms with their meanings and one example. The direction is what students reverse.
lines: 3. The code is UNAMBIGUOUS and SPECIFIC: one
codon codes for ONE amino acid and no other.
4. The code is DEGENERATE: some amino acids are
coded by MORE THAN ONE codon.
Example: leucine has six codons.
Degeneracy follows from having 61 codons for
only 20 amino acids.
steps.why: Sixty-one codons sharing out twenty amino acids means some amino acids must have several codons, so degeneracy is forced by the arithmetic.
common_mistakes: Saying degenerate means one codon codes for several amino acids. It is the other way round: several codons code for ONE amino acid.
Treating unambiguous and degenerate as contradictory. They are not — read them in opposite directions.
steps.memory_tip: One codon, one amino acid; but one amino acid, several codons.

steps.label: Continuous and non-overlapping
steps.margin_note: Both named properties plus the reading-frame consequence.
lines: 5. The code is read in a CONTINUOUS fashion,
with no punctuation between codons. It is
therefore called COMMA-LESS.
6. The code is NON-OVERLAPPING: each base
belongs to one codon only.
7. The code has a fixed READING FRAME, so adding
or deleting one base shifts every codon after
it.
steps.why: With no punctuation and no overlap, the reading frame is everything — which is why a single insertion or deletion ruins the whole protein.
common_mistakes: Saying there are commas or gaps between codons. The code is COMMA-LESS.
Saying bases are shared between codons. The code is NON-OVERLAPPING.
steps.memory_tip: No gaps and no sharing, so the frame is everything.

steps.label: Universal, with a start and stops
steps.margin_note: Universality with an example, then AUG and the three stop codons by name.

lines.text: Nearly universal: UUU is phenylalanine in

lines: 8. The code is nearly UNIVERSAL: it is the same
from bacteria to human beings.
Example: UUU codes for phenylalanine in every
organism.
9. AUG is the INITIATION codon and also codes
for methionine.
10. UAA, UAG and UGA are the STOP codons.
steps.why: The code being the same in every organism is the strongest single piece of evidence that all life shares one ancestor — and it is why a human gene works in a bacterium.
common_mistakes: Saying the code is completely universal. It is NEARLY universal; mitochondria have a few exceptions.
Leaving out the three stop codons by name. UAA, UAG and UGA are expected.
steps.memory_tip: One code for all life, with one start and three stops.
